Your brief follows in the first message.

toolsAdded.name: paint
toolsAdded.description: Run a chunk of Lua at the easel (notes/easel_guide.md). The reply is what the chunk printed, then `ok · chunk N`. A chunk that stops with an error changes nothing.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), shown at 1:1 pixels. mode: "value", "squint", "mirror" or several, comma-separated. size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units.

toolsAdded.name: note
toolsAdded.description: Add an entry to your journal, notes/journal.md, stamped with the painting's time. To revise what is already there, give the exact passage to change as `replaces`: `text` takes its place.

toolsAdded.name: status
toolsAdded.description: The number of chunks, the canvas width in pixels and the canvas's setup.

toolsAdded.name: log
toolsAdded.description: The painting so far: every chunk that ran, in order (paintings/lua/painting.lua).

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original landscape in the manner of Caspar David
Friedrich, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place,
subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the
notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image models or pictures
of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- You paint at the easel: paint a chunk, look at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

## Your journal (notes/journal.md)

Your own notes, quoted as you wrote them:

> - day 1, 09:08: Painting 1: tall portrait (1000x1389 units, 480mm wide). Invented scene: a drowned birch wood at dusk — dark near trunks framing the left, a low bank with a fallen birch and a small standing figure at lower right, still water, a grove of bare birches rising out of mist, a low ridge beyond, a pale evening sky. Working method from the research note: fine linen, warm ground under a lead-white top, precise pencil drawing, then one very thin underpainting in diluted monochrome, then one or two thin colour layers, gradation by stippling and by paint pooling, not by thick blending.
> - day 7, 18:53: Session so far. The picture is a drowned birch wood at dusk: two dark near birches cut by the left edge, a broad evening sky of glazed cloud bands, a luminous band of vapour on the water, a stand of bare birches with their reflections, a wide calm foreground water with a small boat, and a low bank with a fallen birch and a woman standing at the water's edge.
>
>   What the easel taught me, in order, mostly the hard way:
>   - A thin glaze over the warm ground gives olive or pink, not the colour of the pile. To get a real dark or a real cool I had to lay an opaque film (medium 0.02, coverage 2.5+) and lay it again; glazes alone never reached the value I wanted.
>   - `work` with the body hand leaves dabs ("cottage cheese"), especially with opaque paint; `hand="glaze"` lays even films, and a `blend` over the result gives the smooth, slightly slick surface that reads as still water. Stipple at width ~3 gives the fine even grain that suits a Friedrich-like surface.
>   - Long strokes run dry: a 500-unit drag from a full load leaves a blob at the start and streaks after. Long shapes need short segments with a reload, or `work` over a ribbon mask with high coverage and frequent dips.
>   - Every glaze over the midground buried the grove again. The wood has been repainted more times than I care to count; the lesson is to paint the mist first and the wood last, once.
>   - Painting a pale halo beside a dark trunk and then cutting it back is a trap: the pale paint drags the wet dark inward. The eraser lifted the trunks themselves when I tried it (the mask reached under the ragged edges). What finally worked was glazing the background back over a wide band and stippling to match the surrounding texture.
>   - A pass over a mask clips its own boundary, not the picture's: the figure was buried twice by passes meant for the water.
>   - Reflections want to be darker than the water just above them and lighter than the object; where they were pale they read as white drips, where they were stacked too many times they went black.
> - day 14, 17:03: I called it finished on day 14. That was a false finish — looking at it again with fresh eyes a few days later, three things were still wrong with it (see day 15). The last third of the work was one long lesson in restraint: every glaze laid over the midground buried the wood again, and every opaque film laid to fix the water buried the trunks, the boat and the figure in turn. The order that finally worked was water first, wood on top of it, reflections last, and after that nothing more over the middle distance.
>
>   What I would do differently from the start: decide the value of each passage once (dark wood or pale wood, dark water or light) and stick to it. The reflections are the clearest case — I painted them dark while the trunks were dark, then the trunks became pale and the reflections stayed dark and read as brown sticks in the water. They only stopped looking like floating debris when they were repainted pale, straight down, unbroken.
>
>   At the end: a thin glaze over the whole canvas to bind the passages, and the wood drawn back into the vapour with a light veil so it reads as a grove in mist rather than a row of posts.
>
>   The picture: a flooded birch wood at evening. Two dark birches cut by the left edge, a broad sky glazed with warm cloud bands, a luminous band of vapour on the far water where a stand of pale birches stands with its reflections, open water with a small boat and two mooring stakes, and a low bank with a fallen birch, where a woman in a dark coat stands at the water's edge, seen from behind.
> - day 14, 17:03: day 15. Back to the picture after a night's rest and looking at it with fresh eyes, I find three faults that stop it being finished, however well the bones are laid:
>
>   1. The reflections read as white candles. I laid them with a pile of nearly pure lead white at full load, so each one is a hard bright drip with a pointed foot, brighter than anything around it. A reflection in still water is never lighter than the water it lies in; it is a soft, broken grey, cut across by the ripple strokes. They must be redrawn last, in a value between the water and the wood, in two or three lengths with gaps between, and the water's horizontal strokes must then be run across them.
>   2. The two near birches are barred like a ladder. The dark film over them never covered: the pale sky came through the gaps in horizontal bars, and I read them as rungs. A trunk must be an even, opaque body drawn down in short overlapping segments, with the light down one side of it, not a mask filled at random.
>   3. The near bank is a white chop of hard strokes across the bottom of the canvas — torn paper, not a shore. The log has gone into it. The bank wants to be one dark mass with a soft mist along its upper edge and the fallen birch lying clear on top of it.
>
>   Also: the water is woolly — long coarse white scumble over a mauve ground, too much contrast, and the figure is a lumpy bundle with a white scratch down it like a cigarette.
>
>   Order of work, the one my journal keeps pointing to: water first, then the wood, then the reflections, and then nothing over the middle distance at all.
> - day 19, 16:58: day 19. Finished, and this time I mean it. "Flooded Birch Wood (Evening)".
>
>   The picture: two dark birches cut by the left edge, a broad evening sky glazed with cream and blue-grey cloud, a luminous band of vapour along the far shore, a stand of pale birches standing in still water with a breath of reflection under each of them, open water with a soft swell or two, and a dark near bank with a fallen birch along it, where a woman in a shawl stands at the water's edge, seen from behind.
>
>   Everything the first fourteen days built had to be rebuilt once more, and the second time round the easel taught me things I had not learned the first time:
>
>   - `shake` on a narrow brush is a trap. A wandering hand that is invisible under a 26-unit brush sends the tip of a 3-unit rigger wandering two hundred units: my twigs came out as long diagonal scratches all over the wood and the sky, and I spent three passages burying them. No `shake` on anything finer than a filbert 12.
>   - A mark with a point on it reads as an object, not as part of something. Every trunk I drew with a pressure ramp came out a spindle, a blade, a needle; every reflection I drew short came out a leaf, an almond, a white flame. What finally read: trunks with blunt ends, and a separate wide soft stroke above them to blur the top into the vapour; reflections 150 units long and three times as long as they are wide, only a breath lighter than the water, and laid after the wood and touched by nothing afterwards.
>   - A translucent glaze does not bury a mark; it only greys it. To make the old marks go, an opaque film (medium 0, coverage 2 or more) and then a broad `glaze`-hand pass over it to take out the cushions. Every time I tried to save a passage with a glaze I made a new one.
>   - Never `blend` over ground that abuts a hard dark edge. The badger picked the black off the near birches and dragged it across the sky in comet streaks; I lost a good sky to that and had to lay it again.
>   - For a cool grey, white and pale smalt carry it and umber spoils it: two parts of cobalt in a glaze show as blue dashes, not as coolness. Cobalt is a trace, half a part at most.
>   - `fill=true` leaves cottage cheese. The way out is the same both times: a full opaque coat, then a broad soft pass over it with the glaze hand.
>
>   And the old lesson again, which I had written down on day 7 and still had to learn a third time: decide the value of each passage once and stick to it. Water first, then the wood, then the reflections, then nothing at all over the middle distance. Every fault in this picture came from going back over the middle.
> - day 19, 16:58: day 19, 17:40. Day 19 again, looking at it properly at 1:1 rather than at thumbnail size. I have to reverse the last entry. This is not finished; it is the best I have managed, and it is not good enough.
>
>   What is actually wrong, measured rather than felt:
>
>   1. The whole picture sits between about 70 and 95 in value. Sky, mist, water and reflections are the same milky grey-white, so there is no light and no dark anywhere except the two near trunks and the bank. A Friedrich gets his depth from a stacked value range: a dark foreground mass, a dark middle, and one or two places where the light is allowed to be genuinely luminous. I have one light and it is everywhere, so it is nowhere.
>   2. The stand of birches is nineteen pointed pale sticks. They have points on top, flat caps, and in places they are lighter than the water they stand in. They read as fence posts, then as a row of candles. This is exactly the fault my day-15 note described — blunt ends, no points — and it has come back, because a stroke drawn short with a pressure ramp ends in a point whatever I intend.
>   3. The two near birches are black slabs with a hard ragged edge, running the full height of the canvas with no taper, no light side, no branches. They are not trees, they are two bars of the window frame. And there is nothing on the left third of the picture to hold them.
>   4. Those dark horizontal dashes scattered through the mist are not clouds or reflections. They are dirt. There are about thirty of them at unrelated heights and they read as flies on the lens.
>   5. The figure is a black chess pawn. The bank below it is a black shapeless mass with a brown smear on it; the fallen birch has gone.
>
>   So: the composition (a flooded birch wood at evening, dark trees left, luminous far shore, a wood standing in still water, a dark bank with a small figure) is sound and it is mine to keep. The execution has to be taken back to the ground. My own rule — decide the value of each passage once and stick to it — is the rule I broke; everything above is a consequence of it.
>
>   The order, which is the order my journal has been pointing at for three sessions:
>
>     - sky first, deepening upward, so the horizon band can be the light;
>     - then the water, at a value clearly below the mist, all over from the far shore to the near bank — an opaque film, because that is the only thing that kills the sticks and the dashes; the glaze only greys them, as I learned on day 19;
>     - then the luminous mist band, wet into the sky above and the water below;
>     - then the bank;
>     - then the wood, drawn last and once, in a value between the mist and the water, with blunt ends and a soft wide blur above them so the tops go into the vapour;
>     - then the reflections, laid straight down, broken, a breath off the water;
>     - then the two near birches, given a light side and a few bare branches;
>     - the figure last of all, small;
>     - and then nothing at all over the middle distance.
> - day 29, 06:21: day 28, 03:20. I have taken the painting back to the ground and rebuilt it, and the easel taught me five things the first nineteen days did not.
>
>   1. Coverage is not film. `work` at coverage 10 lays about the same thin film as coverage 3. What builds a body is doing the pass again — three separate calls of coverage 3 reach a true dark; one call of coverage 10 does not. Every dark passage in this picture that came out grey was one pass, and every one that came out right was three. My old notes kept saying "lay an opaque film, coverage 2 or more" and that was wrong; it is three passes of 2 or more.
>   2. `edge="soft"` on `work` is a loaded brush. It carried pale paint in a long stroke clear across the canvas, from the near birches to the far wood, and I spent three chunks failing to bury it — three passes of grey, then three of hatch, before it went. From here on: `edge="found"` everywhere on `work`, and where I want a soft passage I blur the mask instead and let the brush stay inside it.
>   3. `below(curve)` and `above(curve)` do not combine with `*` or `-`; `below - below` returns nothing at all, and it fails silently rather than erroring. A band is `below(lo) * above(hi)`, but the safe way is my own `mask(function(x, y) ... end)` with a noise term on the boundary. Also `-m`, not `1 - m`.
>   4. `coverage` cannot be given a function here — the sampler fails converting it to f32 — so a gradient has to be built from two or three separate passes over masks with very wide overlaps, and they must share one pile, or the overlaps show as steps.
>   5. A ribbon takes exactly one width per point. Forgetting that cost me four failed chunks and a rebuild each time.
>
>   And the painterly lesson underneath them, which is the old one again: I spent the best part of three days painting over my own mistakes one at a time, and what actually rescued the picture was deciding to repaint a whole zone cleanly — water, then wood, then reflections, in that order, once — instead of touching up. A fix that is a passage is cheaper than a fix that is a patch.
> - day 299, 11:55: day 299, 10:40. I have stopped. The picture is a flooded birch wood at evening.
>
>   What it is, finally: two dark birches cut by the left edge, bare branches across the evening sky; a sky laid in broad grey and cream cloud bands with the last warmth along the horizon; a band of vapour lying on the far water, the lightest thing in the picture; a stand of bare birches standing in the flood, their tops drawn back into that vapour and their reflections running down under them; open water with a dozen drawn ripples; and a near bank with a fallen birch on it, a few tufts and pebbles, and a small figure in a dark coat standing at the water's edge, seen from behind.
>
>   It is much better than the painting I inherited, and it is not what I would have made in a month. Here is what the second half of this session taught me, and most of it is the opposite of what my earlier notes said:
>
>   - The pile was never the problem. Coverage is not film and my old note "lay it again, coverage 2 or more" was half right and half wrong: it is three or four separate passes, and it only buries something if the paint is opaque. Pale smalt has a hiding of 0.35; a pile that is a third smalt is a third transparent, and no number of passes over it will hide anything. The covers that worked were raw umber and bone black — almost pure hiding pigments. The covers that failed for weeks were my pretty sky greys.
>   - Wet paint does not take a new film, it takes the new colour. I laid passage after passage on top of tacky paint for days and kept getting pale mottled darks and wondering why. Ten days between sessions, and most of the failures simply went away.
>   - A narrow repaint is worse than a wide one. Every time I covered a bad patch with a small mask I left a ridge; a ridge catches the light and comes back when the paint dries, and thin films conform to it instead of hiding it. A broad band of thin paint over the whole field leaves nothing proud. That is why the sky and the water look right and everything I fixed with a small brush still shows.
>   - Three tools bit me and each of them twice: `edge="soft"` on `work` (it carried paint right across the canvas), `stipple` without `clip` (it ignores its own mask), and the badger anywhere near a hard dark edge. I had written all three down already. Writing a lesson down is not the same as having learned it; it took losing the sky to each of them before it stuck.
>   - The last thing I should have done on day 19 was throw the picture away. The composition was the only thing worth keeping, and I spent a hundred and fifty chunks learning that the easiest way to keep a composition is to repaint everything on it.
>
>   If I began again: decide the value of every passage first, in a list, and never let a passage change value afterwards. Decide which colours are opaque and keep smalt under a fifth of every pile. Repaint a whole field or leave a passage alone — never a patch. And let the canvas dry before touching it.

480 chunks · 2400px · size=480, aspect=0.72, linen={14, 12}, seed=41

# The easel

The easel is a live oil painting. You send it Lua chunks with its `paint`
tool, one at a time, and look at the canvas between them with `look`. Under it is a physical paint simulator: simulated
bristles carry wet paint over a primed linen canvas, the paint levels and
dries on a clock, and layers combine by Kubelka–Munk optics.

Three things hold for every session:

- **Every chunk that runs stays on the canvas.** There is no undo. To
  change something, paint over it, or lift wet paint off with a brush.
- **A chunk that stops with an error changes nothing.** The canvas, your
  variables, the paint on your brushes and the clock are as they were
  before it, and it isn't written to the log.
- **The log is the painting.** Every chunk that ran is appended to
  `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, and replaying it paints the same canvas.

## Starting

The studio holds one painting, and the easel is open on it. Its tools:

| tool | what it does |
|---|---|
| `paint` | runs a chunk of Lua. The reply is what the chunk printed, then `ok · chunk N` |
| `look` | shows you the canvas as it is now (see [Looking](#looking)) |
| `note` | adds an entry to your journal (see [The journal](#the-journal)) |
| `status` | the number of chunks, the canvas width in pixels and the canvas's setup |
| `log` | the painting so far: every chunk that ran, each after a line `--@ chunk N` |

The first chunk is `canvas{}` (see [The canvas](#the-canvas)). The canvas
is 2400 pixels wide. `read` reads the files in this folder: your brief and
your notes.

In the examples below, `<tube>` stands for a name from the tube box and
`<parts>` for a number of parts you choose. Other numbers in the examples
only show how a call is written; they aren't recommended values.

## The canvas

```lua
canvas{size=<mm>, aspect=<width / height>, linen={<warp>, <weft>}, seed=<seed>,
       ground={{pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=<µm>, apply="<how>", texture=<0..1>},
               ...}}
```

- `size`: the canvas's width in mm (50 to 5000).
- `aspect`: width / height.
- `linen`: plain-weave linen, threads per cm, one number or `{warp, weft}`
  (4 to 60).
- `ground`: the preparation layers, bottom first. Each is a paste mixed
  from tubes in parts (as a pile is, below), a thickness in µm (5 to 400)
  and how it is put on: `"knife"` (levels the weave; `texture` 0..1 is the
  knife's waviness), `"roller"` (a fine even texture) or `"brush"` (laid in
  crossing strokes, its striations stay). The ground is dry when painting
  starts.
- `seed`: the randomness of the linen, the ground and everything after.

It sets `W` (1000) and `H` (`1000 / aspect`). The canvas is always 1000
units wide, whatever its pixel width. The origin `(0, 0)` is the upper
left corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Angles are radians,
0 left to right, π/2 downward.

## Tubes and piles

Paint reaches the canvas only from piles you knife together on the
palette from the tubes in the box:

```lua
p = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}
q = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, medium=0.3}
print(p)                         -- pile(<tube> <parts>, <tube> <parts>; medium 0)
print(table.concat(tubes(), ", "))   -- the names in the box
```

A pile is parts by volume of named tubes, plus `medium`: the share of oil
medium mixed in (0, as from the tube, to 0.95). Medium makes the paint more
transparent and more fluid, and slower to dry. It is added oil only. What a pile looks like is
what its pigments make together, thick or thin, over what is already on
the canvas; you find out by painting with it and looking. A pile mixed by
hand is a little uneven: each brushload takes slightly different
proportions (about 6%). The palette has room for 16 piles; the oldest is
scraped off to make room.

The tube box:

| tube | pigment | hiding | stiffness | tinting strength | drying |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lead white | basic lead carbonate | 0.82 | 0.8 | 1.0 | 2.0 |
| smalt | cobalt potash glass, coarse | 0.3 | 0.55 | 0.45 | 1.6 |
| pale smalt | a paler grade of smalt | 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.35 | 1.6 |
| yellow ochre | hydrated iron oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.7 | 0.8 | 0.8 |
| red earth | iron oxide earth | 0.85 | 0.7 | 0.9 | 1.0 |
| vermilion | mercuric sulfide | 0.9 | 0.75 | 1.0 | 0.4 |
| raw umber | iron and manganese oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.65 | 0.9 | 2.4 |
| bone black | charred bone (carbon, calcium phosphate) | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.1 | 0.4 |
| cobalt blue | cobalt aluminate | 0.55 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 1.4 |
| chrome yellow | lead chromate | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.0 | 1.8 |
| Prussian blue | iron ferrocyanide | 0.35 | 0.45 | 3.0 | 1.8 |
| green earth | celadonite and glauconite clay | 0.2 | 0.35 | 0.3 | 0.8 |
| Rinmann's green | cobalt-zinc oxide | 0.35 | 0.5 | 0.4 | 1.4 |
| copper green | verdigris ground in oil | 0.25 | 0.4 | 1.0 | 1.6 |

Hiding is how much one coat of the tube paint hides what is under it (0
transparent, 1 opaque). Stiffness is the paint's body as it comes from the
tube (0 fluid, 1 stiff). Tinting strength is relative to an average
pigment. Drying is the rate relative to average paint (higher dries
faster); a pile dries at its tubes' rates mixed by volume. These numbers
are estimates from the pigment literature, not measurements.

## Brushes and strokes

```lua
b = brush("filbert", 8)                  -- kinds: round, flat, filbert, fan, rigger, badger, stippler
b = brush{kind="round", width=3, point=1, stiffness=0.5}   -- also length, hair, run, lay, pickup,
                                                           -- push, splay, ragged, bristles
b:load(p, 0.8)                           -- dip into a pile: 0..1 of a full load
b:reload(q, 0.8)                         -- wipe most of the old paint off, then load
b:wipe(0.85)                             -- remove 85% of the paint onto the rag
b:fullness()                             -- paint left, 0..1
b:stroke({{120, 640}, {260, 470}, {430, 420}},
  {pressure={0.9, 0.3}, ramps={0.05, 0.4}, orient="across", shake=1, swell={1, 1.3, 0.8}, clip=m})
b:touch(400, 300, {pressure=0.6, drag={1, 0}, twist=0.2, angle=0.3, clip=m})
b:mark_width(0.4)                        -- the width of a mark at this pressure (units)
b:pressure_for(0.5)                      -- the pressure for a 0.5-unit line
```

Widths are in canvas units. A brush keeps its paint across strokes and
chunks, so strokes from one load run dry, and a brush that has been
through wet paint carries some of it. Pressure ranges from 0 (lifted)
to 1 (fully pressed); a stroke's `pressure` is `{start, end}`.
`ramps` gives the press-down and lift-off fractions, `swell` pressure factors
along the stroke, `orient` `"across"`, `"along"` or a fixed angle.

Brushes are blunt unless given a `point` (0 blunt, 1 a full point). A
pointed round or rigger lays a hairline at light pressure and spreads to
its belly when pressed, so its width follows the pressure and a stroke
whose pressure falls to 0 ends in a point.

## Covering an area

```lua
work(m, {hand="<hand>", pile=p, angle=<radians>, coverage=<layers>})
blend(m, {angle=<radians>})              -- a clean blender over wet paint (= work with hand="blend")
stipple(m, {pile=p, width=<units>, coverage=<layers>})
work(m, {hand="glaze", pile=q})          -- a thin layer brushed on with a soft brush
lose(m, {pile=p, where=0.5})
```

`work` covers a mask with strokes of a real brush, planned the way a hand
lays them. `hand` picks a starting handling, which the options below
change:

| hand | tool | strokes |
|---|---|---|
| `broad` | filbert 22 | 80–220 units, bowing in long arcs, direction wandering over 350-unit patches |
| `body` (default) | filbert 9 | 20–60 units |
| `detail` | round 2.2 | 4–14 units, clipped to the mask |
| `hatch` | round 2.6 | 5–12 units, nearly straight, side by side, clumped |
| `glaze` | soft filbert 26 | 120–300 units, light pressure |
| `scumble` | filbert 9 | 10–20 units, worked back and forth |
| `blend` | badger 40 | a clean blender, crossing passes top to bottom, inside the mask |

| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `pile` | the pile every stroke dips into (every hand but `blend`) |
| `tool` | `"filbert 8"`, `{kind=, width=, ...}` or a brush |
| `length` | `{min, max}` stroke length in units |
| `coverage` | layers of strokes over each point on average |
| `angle` | stroke direction: a number or `function(x, y)` |
| `pressure`, `ramps` | `{min, max}` pressure; attack and release fractions |
| `dips` | `{strokes per trip to the palette, load, wipe before dipping}` |
| `load`, `load_at` | load per dip; a number or `function(x, y)` that varies it |
| `edge` | how the passage meets the mask's edge (below) |
| `clip` | `true`: every bristle stops on the mask's edge; or a mask to clip to |
| `hug` | `true` (default): strokes reach the mask's edges; `false` lets coverage thin there |
| `fill` | `false` by default: gaps between strokes stay. Set `true` to follow the strokes with dabs into the gaps they left |
| `order` | `"passages"` (default), `"scatter"`, `"down"`, `"across"` or a sweep angle |
| `angle_jitter`, `curve` (`{bow, wave}`), `cross`, `drift` (`{amount, scale}`), `tail`, `broken`, `swell`, `clump`, `ruler` | how far the strokes depart from even ruler lines (`ruler=true` sets them straight and even) |
| `orient`, `shake`, `threshold`, `cut_in` (a tool), `scrub`, `blender`, `mix_jitter`, `seed` | the brush's orientation, the hand's unsteadiness, the mask level strokes are anchored at, cutting in the edge with a second tool, back-and-forth strokes, a clean brush, how uneven each dip of the pile is, the randomness |

Where an option takes `function(x, y)`, it is sampled every 2 units over
the area and interpolated. A mistyped option is an error that lists the
valid ones.

**What stays inside the mask.** `work` plans its strokes from the mask:
each stroke is anchored in it, but its path can begin outside and cross
the edge. By default `detail` and `blend` keep their paint inside the
mask. The other hands (`body`, `broad`, `hatch`, `glaze`, `scumble`) can
carry paint past the edge onto whatever is there, by as much as a stroke's
length (a `glaze` stroke is 120–300 units by default). `clip=true` keeps
every bristle inside the mask; `clip=` another mask keeps them inside that
one instead. `edge=` (below) shapes how the passage meets the edge, with
an overrun that varies and can reach beyond it.

**Edges.** `edge=` carries the passage up to the mask's edge the way a
brush does: each stroke stops by its own amount, and past the line its
film thins out over the weave. It takes a number from 0 (found: crisp) to
1 (lost: the passage runs well past the line and dissolves), a name
(`"found"`, `"firm"`, `"soft"`, `"loose"`, `"lost"`), a function of
`(x, y)`, a mask, or a table: `{found=, soft=, lost=, period=40, seed=}`
lays those shares out along the contour in runs about `period` units long;
`waver=` and `reach=` scale how far the line wanders and how far strokes
run over. It can't be combined with `cut_in`.

**`stipple(m, {...})`** lays many small touches of a tip, each through the
bristles: `pile`, `width` (a stippler's width, 2 by default) or `tool`,
`coverage` (touches per point; a number or `function(x, y)`), `pressure`
`{min, max}`, `dips` `{touches per dip, load, wipe}`, `drag` (how far the
tip moves while down: a number or `{length, angle}`), `twist`, `cluster`
(0 even .. 1 in clumps, or `{amount, size}`), `feather` (0 by default;
above 0, touches get lighter where coverage is below 1), `clip`,
`mix_jitter`, `seed`.

**`lose(m, {pile=, where=, ...})`** drags a lightly loaded brush across
the mask's edge from the outside in, where `where` (as `edge=`; 1 by
default) is high: short strokes start outside, cross the edge at a slant
(or at `angle`) and lift off inside. Also `tool` (`"filbert 4"`), `reach`
(`{out, in}` units), `load` (0.2), `pressure` (`{0.35, 0.02}`), `every`
(a stroke every 1.2 brush widths), `seed`. It returns the number of
strokes.

`work`, `blend` and `stipple` also take `visible=`, `behind=`,
`at=` and `view=` (see [Depth](#depth)).

## Masks and geometry

Masks are coverage maps (0..1) of the whole canvas. Operations return new
masks.

```lua
everywhere()   rect(x, y, w, h)   ellipse(cx, cy, rx, ry)
poly({{x, y}, ...})   poly(pts, true)                  -- true: smoothed
below(function(x) return 150 + 0.6 * x end)   -- under a curve (or a point list)
above(curve)
ribbon(points, widths)   ribbon(points, 3)             -- a band along a line
mask(function(x, y) return x < 500 and 1 or 0 end)    -- any function, at every pixel
m + n   m * n   m - n   -m                             -- union, intersection, difference, inverse
m:roughen(units, period, seed, edge)   m:soften(units)   m:blur(units)
m:grow(units)   m:shrink(units)   m:offset(units)   m:rim(width, soft)
m:distance()   m:band(lo, hi, soft)   m:times(fn or mask)   m:map(function(v) return v * v end)
m:at(x, y)   m:area()
```

Points are `{{x, y}, ...}` or a flat `{x1, y1, x2, y2, ...}`.

Numbers and randomness: `rand(a, b)`, `randn(mean, sd)`, `math.random`,
`lerp(a, b, t)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `smoothstep(a, b, x)`;
`noise{seed=, octaves=4, period=200, persistence=0.5, kind="fbm"|"ridged"|"billow", warp={period, amount, twice}, stretch={angle, k}}`
(call it as `n(x, y)` for about -1..1, `n:at01(x, y)` for 0..1; it can be
passed to `coverage=` or `load_at=`); `worley{seed=, period=, jitter=}`
(`c:at(x, y)` gives the distances to the nearest two cell points, how near
a cell wall, and a stable 0..1 per cell); `uneven(n, lo, hi, irregular,
clump, seed)` (n positions from lo to hi with uneven, clumped gaps).

**Drawn lines.** `outline{pts... or pts=, char=, seed=, closed=, open=,
corners=, corner_angle=60, size=, amount=, lobe=, edge=}` turns a few
points into a line drawn by hand (a smooth curve through them, broken at
corners marked `"c"`, with a hand's irregularity) and its mask:

```lua
o = outline{{300, 600, "c"}, {320, 450}, {420, 380, "c"}, {560, 400}, {650, 480, "c"}, {500, 620}, char="firm", seed=3}
work(o:mask(), {hand="body", pile=p})
o:paint(b, {pressure=0.8, dip={p, 0.6}, every=3})   -- stroke the line itself
```

| char | the line |
|---|---|
| `firm` (default for `outline`) | long strokes, slight overshoots, a crisp mask |
| `searching` | short strokes restated a little off each other, running past corners |
| `broken` | straight facets and chips in broken stretches between quiet ones |
| `soft` (default for `body_of`) | lobes of two sizes, light broken strokes, a mask edge lost in places |

`amount` scales the irregularity (0 is a clean curve), `lobe` sets the
lobe width in units, `edge` the mask's soft edge in units. An open line's
outside is on its left. `body_of{spine=, widths=, limbs={{pts..., widths=}, ...}, blend=0.8, char=}`
is the silhouette of a skeleton of points and widths. Methods: `o:mask()`,
`o:below(bottom)`, `o:above()`, `o:band(width, taper)`, `o:inset(d)`,
`o:offset(d)`, `o:paint(brush, {...})`, `o:path(i)`, `o:paths()`,
`o:strokes()`, `o:at(t)`, `o:length()`, `o:corners()`.

## Drawing: pencil, chalk and eraser

```lua
h = pencil("2H")                  -- or pencil{grade="2H"}: 9H..H, F, HB, B..9B
c = chalk()                       -- black chalk
h:sketch(pts, {pressure=0.3})     -- a few light passes (passes=3, wander= units, smooth=true)
h:line(pts, {pressure={0.5, 0.7, 0.4}})    -- one line through the points (smooth=false keeps corners)
h:rule({120, 700}, {860, 180}, {pressure=0.3})  -- straight, against a ruler
h:hatch(m, {angle=-1.1, pressure=0.35})         -- short parallel strokes (spacing=, length=)
h:width()   h.worn   h:sharpen()  -- the point blunts as you draw
erase(pts, {strength=0.9, width=9})  -- a kneaded eraser along a path, or erase(mask, {strength=})
fix()                                -- fixative (or fix(mask)): the eraser no longer lifts it
drawing_guide()                      -- the drawn lines themselves, as a continuous mask
```

The point rides on the tops of the weave; pressure lets it reach into the
hollows. Soft leads lay darker, glossier lines, hard ones pale silver
lines. The eraser lifts most of a line, more from the tops than the
hollows, and leaves a ghost. Once paint has gone over the drawing it is
sealed: thin paint lets it show through, body paint hides it.

## Solids, light and space

These are scaffolds for shapes you give them: they answer where light
and shadow fall and what lies in front of what.

**Form.** Solids in canvas units, z toward you, lit by one light:

```lua
s = body.ellipsoid({400, 500, 0}, {120, 90, 80}):turn({400, 500, 0}, 0.3, 0.1, 0)
      :cut({400, 430, 0}, {-0.3, -1, 0.4}, 1, 3):rough(6, 120, 1)
k = body.block({650, 520, 0}, {160, 60, 90}, 3)       -- center, size, rounding
t = terrain{area={250, 200, 650, 500}, height=function(x, y) return 10 * math.sin(x / 60) end}
f = form{ {s, dist=0.3}, {k}, light={from={-1, -0.7}, front=0.5, ambient=0.2} }
f:value(x, y)   f:lit_at(x, y, soft)   f:part(x, y)   f:sample(x, y)   f:fall(x, y)   f:across(x, y)
f:lit{parts={1}, soft=0.12}   f:shadow{parts={1}}   f:silhouette{parts={1}}   f:edges{turn=0.8}   f:parts_mask{1}
work(f:lit{parts={1}}, {pile=p, angle=f:field("fall")})   -- field("fall"|"across"|"edge") for angle=
```

Solids combine with `s:union(o)` and `s:subtract(o)`; `body.half_space(at,
normal)` cuts. The light also takes `bounce`, `bounce_from`, `penumbra`,
`reach`, `thickness` and `across_parts`.

**World (reference).** A space in meters seen in perspective: a camera
over a supporting surface, one directional light, and the bodies you
place there. Its calls:

```lua
w = world{eye=<m>, fov=<degrees>}        -- camera height and field of view
s = w:spot(x, y)                         -- the surface seen at a canvas point (or w:spot_at(X, Z))
w, n = w:place(s, body.block(s:p(0, 0.5, 0), s:size(1, 1, 1), s:m(0.05)))   -- s:p, s:size, s:m: meters to units
v = w:view()                             -- trace once and keep it
v:bodies_mask{n}   v:shadows()   v:contact(0.25)   v:at(x, y)   v.form
w:to_ground(x, y)   w:project(X, Y, Z)   w:scale_at(Z)   w:height(x, y, meters)
w:shadow_angle(x, y)   w:sun_canvas()   w:ribbon(pts, width)   w:recede({X, Z}, {dX, dZ}, n)
```

`world{}` options, all optional: `view` (the canvas rectangle it
covers), `horizon` (the canvas y of eye level), `eye`, `fov`, `ground` (a
function `(X, Z)` giving the surface's height in meters; flat by
default), `water` (`{level=, ripple=}`: a level reflecting surface),
`sun` (`{azimuth=, elevation=}` in degrees: the light's direction;
azimuth 0 is straight ahead, -90 to the left, 180 behind the eye),
`visibility` and `backdrop`. View queries: `v:water()` and `v:mirror(x,
y)` (with `water`), `v:land()` and `v:sky()` (where the surface and the
space above it are seen). `w:proxy(s, body)` places a body that casts a
shadow but isn't seen. `w:aerial(Z)` and `aerial(dist, visibility)` give
how much air lies between the eye and a distance (0..1).

**Depth.** A view knows what lies behind what. `w = w:layer(name, mask,
depth)` registers a shape you paint by hand at a depth (meters, a spot, a
canvas point `{x, y}` where it stands on the ground, or `"ground"`); make
the view after it. Then `v:visible(x)`, `v:front(x)`, `v:behind(x)`,
`v:at_depth(m)`, `v:between(a, b)` and `v:seen(x, y)` are masks and
answers, and `v:cast_shadow{soft=, from=}` and `v:contact_shadow{reach=,
from=}` are shadows that fall off with distance from what casts them.
Things are named by body number, layer name, `"ground"`, `"water"`,
`"surface"`, `"sky"`, `"bodies"`, `"layers"`, a mask or a list. Passes take
`visible=` (only where that is seen), `behind=` (only where nothing in
front of it is) and `at=` (a depth in meters): strokes still overrun the
mask's own edges, never what is in front.

## Time

Painting takes time, and paint dries on the painting's clock. Only
painting operations (strokes, touches, passes, trips to the palette) and
`wait(minutes)` advance it. Real time between chunks does not: paint
doesn't dry while you think. `wait(minutes)` passes painting time at once;
it doesn't make you wait that many real minutes.

- **Hand time.** Every stroke, touch, pass and trip to the palette takes
  the time a hand takes to make it: a stroke by its length and the
  brush's width (broad sweeps are fast, fine lines slow per mm), a
  stipple touch about a third of a second, a dip into a pile on the
  palette 2.5 s, knifing a new pile 20 s. The paint ages while the hand
  works: a long pass is painted in slices of 15 minutes, and its first
  strokes are setting by the time the last go on.
- **`wait(minutes)`** lets time pass with your hand away from the canvas:
  minutes, hours or days (`wait(3 * 24 * 60)`), up to 10 years
  (5,259,600 minutes). It returns the time of day, e.g. `day 3, 14:20`
  (the painting was begun at 09:00 on day 1).
- **`drying(x, y)`** tells you what the paint there is like to the touch:
  `"open"` (workable: it blends and lifts), `"setting"` (stiff, barely
  blends), `"tacky"` (set; it grabs the brush) or `"dry"` (touch-dry).

Each film dries at its own pace, set by its pigments, its thickness and
its oil. Thin lean paint of fast-drying pigments is touch-dry in a day;
thick, oily paint of slow pigments can stay open for weeks. Wet paint
under a new stroke comes up into it; paint laid over dry paint sits on
top of it.

## Looking

`look` shows you the canvas as it is now, with wet paint as laid. The live canvas is 2400 pixels wide. A whole view is
scaled down to at most 1600 pixels on its long side and kept below 3 MB,
like stepping back. A crop shows the original pixels at 1:1 and may be
at most 1200 pixels on either side. `crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1"` gives two
opposite corners in canvas units, not a position and width/height.

| `look` with | shows |
|---|---|
| nothing | the whole canvas, scaled down |
| `crop: "300,200,500,350"` | a window in canvas units, at 1:1 pixels |
| `mode: "value"` | in grays |
| `mode: "squint"` | blurred, as through half-closed eyes |
| `mode: "mirror"` | flipped left to right |
| `mode: "value,squint"`, `size: 600` | modes combine; `size` sets the long side |
| `grid: true` | a squared grid in canvas units, labeled along the edges |
| `crop: "300,200,500,350"`, `grid: 10` | a window with a grid every 10 units |

The grid is drawn on the PNG only, never on the canvas, like the squares
ruled over a drawing to transfer it.

## How chunks behave

- **Globals persist, locals don't.** Each chunk is its own Lua chunk:
  `p = pile{...}` is there in later chunks, `local p = ...` is not.
- **Randomness is deterministic.** `math.random`, `rand` and `randn` are
  reseeded at the start of every chunk from the canvas's seed and the
  chunk's number, and passes pick their own seeds the same way (pass
  `seed=` to fix one). A replay paints the same thing, and a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

# Studio notes

Observations of the canvas, the paint and the tools at this easel, by
operation: what was done, what the paint did and, where it's known, why.
Each was seen under particular conditions and may be incomplete or wrong.
They describe the easel; they aren't instructions. Widths and positions
are in canvas units (the canvas is 1000 units wide).

## The canvas and ground

1. The linen's vertical threads are more even than the horizontal ones,
   which carry thick slubs a few millimeters long; their spacing follows the
   counts set in `canvas{}`.
2. The ground chosen in `canvas{}` shows through thin paint; body color
   hides it.
3. Light paint laid at light pressure over a wet dark catches only the high
   points of a knife-textured ground. The dark stays in the hollows as a
   net of fine dark lines that looks like cracking.
4. Bristles plough paint off the tops of the weave, so a lay-in can keep
   small specks of bare ground. A denser pass covers them.

## Paint in thin films

5. A coat of paint over paint of its own masstone looks the same at any
   thickness, so a mark from a pile matching what it lies on disappears
   into it.
6. A thin film doesn't look like its pile. Thin dark or earth mixtures over
   a pale passage come out lighter, warmer and more saturated than the
   masstone on the palette.
7. The thin fringe of an umber or black stroke over a light field dries
   as a warm brown to warm gray halo. A blue stroke's fringe stays blue.
8. Lead white hides strongly (its hiding in the guide's tube table is
   0.82; how much a coat covers also depends on its thickness). A thin veil of a pale
   lead-white mixture veils and lightens what is under it, like a scumble,
   rather than tinting it.

## Brushes

9. Every brush is blunt unless given a `point`. A blunt brush's mark runs
   from about half its width at the lightest touch to its full width pressed
   (a little more with splay), so it can't taper to a point.
10. A pointed brush at light pressure lays a hairline, and its width grows
    with pressure. A band a few units wide needs real pressure or a blunt
    brush of that width. A stroke whose pressure falls off at the end draws
    down to the tip and still reaches the end of its path.
11. A brush keeps its paint across strokes. Each stroke lays most at its
    start, and the load runs down along the stroke, so a long drag with a
    wide brush runs dry partway and leaves thinly covered streaks and bands.
12. A well-loaded hair wets the hollows of the weave. A nearly empty one
    skims the tops (dry brush, broken color). Soft hair bends down into the
    hollows; stiff bristle rides on the tops.
13. Whether a dry brush breaks up depends on its load, the pressure, the
    paint below and the ground's texture.
14. A pointed brush loaded below about a quarter stops wetting the hollows,
    and its thin line breaks up along the weave. Run dry, the tip loses its
    point and splits.
15. A pressed touch lays one continuous, nearly round patch (the paint
    bridges the hairs) that grows with pressure.

## Strokes, passes and clipping

16. `clip=true` stops every bristle on the mask's edge, weighted by the
    mask's value. A clipped fill reproduces the mask's outline exactly, as
    one even line, steps and corners included. The `detail` and `blend`
    hands are clipped by default. `broad`, `body`, `hatch`, `glaze` and
    `scumble` are not.
17. Unclipped strokes run past the mask's edge by their own length and
    width. Along a long straight edge they throw small irregular patches into the field
    beyond, and a brush wider than a band spreads well outside it.
18. The square ends of unclipped strokes notch a shape's edge into steps.
19. In `work`, the mask's value decides where strokes are anchored (at or
    above `threshold`: 0.3, or 0.1 for `detail`). Unclipped, a soft mask
    edge doesn't make a soft paint edge; strokes end where their lengths
    end.
20. `work` leaves the ground showing between its strokes. With `fill=true`
    it looks at its passage afterward and dabs paint into the bare spots its
    strokes left. Single `stroke` and `touch` calls don't fill in.
21. Short strokes planned along a band about one unit wide come out as a
    dashed line: the planner lays them separately, with gaps.
22. Parallel strokes that all break at the same places leave a row of stroke
    ends across the passage, and the outer strokes' ends make a lobed edge.
23. `cut_in` with a round along a curved edge lays short strokes that follow
    it as a string of small bumps.
24. In a smooth lean passage, the loaded starts of broad strokes stay as
    lighter patches. Blending reduces them but doesn't remove them.

## Wet into wet

25. A brush over open paint lifts some of it and mixes it with its own. A
    clean brush lifts wet paint, less as it sets, and nothing from set or
    dry paint.
26. Light touches into a wet dark dissolve into it. The same touches on
    paint that has set stay where they land.
27. A pale stroke dragged through a wet dark picks up the dark and comes out
    streaked, grayer and less opaque, so what is underneath shows.
28. A dark stroke laid into a wet pale passage lifts the pale and comes out
    paler than its pile.
29. A passage laid against a wet neighbor drags the neighbor into its edge.
30. Crossing strokes in wet paint thin each other at the crossings, and the
    layer below shows there.
31. A tacky surface grabs: a brush dragged over it leaves its paint sooner
    and in broken patches (stick and slip).

## Stippling

32. Touches into a wet layer lift some of it and fuse. On a dry layer each
    touch stays separate.
33. One dip serves one small patch of touches (24 by default), and each
    dip's mixture varies a little. On a dry layer the passage can dry as a
    patchwork of slightly different patches; fewer touches per dip make the
    patches smaller.
34. Coverage is how many touches fall on each point; one touch covers about
    π(0.4 × width)².
35. Contrast with what is underneath decides how a stipple reads. A coverage
    that gives a veil over a mid tone gives solid patches over a pale field.
36. With `feather` above 0, touches press lighter where coverage falls
    below 1, so a thinning stipple ends in smaller, fainter marks; at 0 they
    keep their pressure.
37. A row of separate touches along a thin line reads as a string of beads.
    A short dragged stroke along it reads as one continuous ridge.

## Blending

38. The blender fuses open paint by lifting it and moving it. It can't move
    set or dry paint.
39. `blend` stays inside its mask by default. Unclipped, it drags wet paint
    across the mask's edge.
40. Touches stippled into a wet layer and then blended fuse into it. Only
    the strongest contrasts survive, as thin traces. Touches laid after the
    blending pass stay on top as a lacy texture.
41. Repeated blending of one lean layer lifts paint off the tops of the
    weave, and the ground shows through as a pale lattice.
42. Blending spreads each thin spot in a layer into a soft-edged patch.

## Glazing

43. A brushed glaze (`hand="glaze"`) isn't clipped.

## Masks

44. Every mask covers the whole canvas. A mask function that isn't zero far
    from the spot you mean paints there too.
45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

# Physics of oil paint on canvas

**Tags.** **[V]**: the number is in the source text. **[S]**: the number is from a summary of the source, not its full text. **[E]**: an estimate or derivation, with its assumptions stated.

---

## 1. Rheology and leveling

**Constitutive behavior.** Tube oil paint is a viscoplastic, shear-thinning and thixotropic suspension. A Herschel–Bulkley law fits it well: τ = τ_y + K·γ̇ⁿ, with n ≈ 0.2–0.7[S].

| Quantity | Value | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yield stress, model ultramarine oil paint (32 vol% solids) | **10–20 Pa**. Brushstrokes came out regular and low-relief (Rz < 100 µm) | [V] |
| Yield stress, same paint + 4 vol% egg yolk (capillary network) | **≈3000–3200 Pa**. Strong impasto, and wrinkling suppressed | [V] |
| Typical tube paints | ~10–1000 Pa; stiff impasto grades above 1000 Pa | [S] |
| Apparent viscosity | 10⁴–10⁷ Pa·s at 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹; 10–10³ Pa·s at 10–100 s⁻¹ (brushing) | [S] |
| Linseed oil (the medium) | η ≈ 0.048 Pa·s, σ ≈ 33–36 mN/m at 20 °C | [S] |
| Stand oil | η ≈ 0.5–25 Pa·s depending on grade | [S] |

Impasto requires "sufficiently high yield stress preventing levelling after brush passage," while brushability depends on the *high-shear* viscosity, so stiff paint can still brush easily[V].

**Orchard leveling (Newtonian, thin film h ≪ λ).** A sinusoidal ridge of wavelength λ on a film of mean thickness h decays as a(t) = a₀·e^(−t/τ), with

  **τ = 3η(λ/2π)⁴ / (σh³)**[V].

The dependence is λ⁴ and h⁻³, so λ and h matter far more than η or σ.

**Yield-stress floor.** Surface tension produces a leveling stress of about 8π³σha/λ³. Flow stops once τ_y exceeds it, so ridges smaller than

  **a_c = τ_y λ³ / (8π³ σ h)**

never level[S]. For thixotropic paint, τ_y(t) recovers after brushing, so leveling starts and then freezes with a residual mark[S]. With solvent evaporation, moderate yield stress can actually reduce residual unevenness[S].

**Worked numbers [E]** (σ = 0.035 N/m):

| Case | η | λ | h | τ (1/e time) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medium-rich glaze, bristle striation | 1 Pa·s | 0.3 mm | 20 µm | 0.06 s |
| Glaze, stroke-scale ridge | 1 Pa·s | 2 mm | 20 µm | 110 s |
| Tube paint, stroke ridge, low-shear η | 10³–10⁴ Pa·s | 2 mm | 100 µm | 15 min – 2.5 h |

| τ_y | Frozen amplitude a_c, λ = 0.3 mm, h = 100 µm | a_c, λ = 2 mm, h = 300 µm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 Pa | ~0.5–1 µm (striations vanish) | ~45 µm |
| 100 Pa | ~3–6 µm | ~300 µm |
| 500 Pa | ~15–30 µm | effectively frozen |
| 3000 Pa | ~90–200 µm | frozen |

The ranges come from comparing the thin-film form with a deep-layer form, a_c ≈ τ_yλ²/(4π²σ), derived for h ≳ λ/2π, where the lubrication assumption fails [E]. **Conclusion:** bristle striations survive only in paint with τ_y ≳ 100 Pa. Fluid glaze paint levels its bristle marks within seconds but can keep mm-scale ridges if it has any yield stress.

## 2. Brush marks

| Fiber | Diameter | Tip | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hog bristle | 0.20–0.30 mm (fine hog 0.15–0.25) | Naturally split ("flagged") | [S] |
| Kolinsky/red sable | ~60–120 µm | Single fine taper | [S] |

In profilometry of oil paintings, the height features that best identify the painter sit at **0.2–0.4 mm**, matching the bristle widths used (**0.25 and 0.65 mm**)[V]. For macro impasto, a 17th-century canvas has measured relief up to about 0.85 mm[S].

**Dry brush and scumble.** A technical description of an 1879/80 canvas reports "an almost dry brush [dragged] across the surface, catching only the thread tops". This works even over a heavy, smooth ground: the deposit follows *contact*, not flow.

## 3. Film formation and drying

- **Mass and skin timeline.** A titanium white in alkali-refined linseed oil (10 mil ≈ 250 µm film) gained nearly **16%** of its oil weight in the first days. It "begins to skin over" as it nears the peak and is touch-dry at **4–6 days**. Cold-pressed and alkali-refined oils peak at **15–18%** and then slowly lose mass over a year or more[V].
- **Skinning and wrinkling.** Oxygen enters through the surface, so a crosslinked skin forms over mobile paint. Wrinkling is a compressive buckle of that skin. It is worse in thick, oil-rich or drier-heavy films[V]. Raising τ_y to about 3200 Pa suppressed wrinkling in model paints[V].
- **Long-term shrinkage and brittleness** (films 21–31 years old, cold-pressed linseed oil)[S]:

| Paint | Cumulative shrinkage | Aged strain at break | Aged modulus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead white | 0.5% | 0.3–0.8% | ~1 GPa |
| Lead white + litharge | 0.9% | 0.5% | ~2.9 GPa |
| Zinc white | 0.3% | 0.1–0.3% | 2–3 GPa |
| Verdigris | 1.7% | 0.1% | — |
| Red iron oxide | ~0% | 0.3% | ~50 MPa |

  Lead white's strain at break fell from **7.3% at 0.2 years** to under 1% at 31 years[S]. Chalk-glue grounds are modeled with a break strain of **0.002**[V].
- **Layer thicknesses.** A three-layer commercial ground from about 1880 measured **1.5–30 µm (chalk), 5–35 µm and 10–45 µm (lead white)**[V]. Mock-up oil layers measured **59–125 µm for one coat** and 110–188 µm for two[S]. Single paint layers run roughly 10–200+ µm [S; general cross-section ranges, low confidence].
- **Conformal vs. filling.** That ground is "thicker and smoother, greatly diminishing the texture of the canvas weave"[V]. Orchard's law explains the physics: with the weave pitch λ ≈ 0.3–0.8 mm, a film only 10–20 µm thick has τ ∝ h⁻³ that is huge, and it may also have a yield floor. Thin paint therefore stays conformal to the weave, while thick fluid paint levels over it [E].

## 4. Canvas and ground

**Thread counts (plain weave unless noted).** These are individual measured paintings, not period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

day 302, 12:40. I drowned the picture in one chunk and then rebuilt it. Here is the whole of what happened, because the mistake is worth more than the painting was.

I found the sky too pale and tried to deepen the zenith with a dark glaze at coverage 1.8. It went almost black, and the glaze strokes skipped over the bright cloud bands and left white scratches: a torn black curtain, not an evening sky. My own notes from day 19 and day 299 said this exact thing would happen — a glaze only greys, and a glaze hand at high coverage over a strong dark is a loaded brush. I did it anyway, at coverage 1.8, in one call.

What I got wrong in my own piles: I kept writing mixtures of lead white with raw umber and bone black and assuming they would come out mid, and they came out near-black every time. The cure was to stop guessing. I laid a strip of four candidate mixtures across the top of the canvas, three passes each, and read their value with `look mode=value`. What I learned: raw umber and bone black are both so dark that almost any mixture with them lands in the forties or below; the mid greys I wanted need lead white as the major part and the earths as a small fraction of it. I had been writing the earths as the major part all along.

So I repainted the whole sky as one even opaque field, five separate passes at coverage 1.6 — the rule from day 28 again: separate calls, not one call at coverage 5 — and then graded the zenith with a genuinely transparent glaze (medium 0.45) at coverage 1.0, which cannot tear because it cannot hide. That worked. The sky is now clean, cool and open, and it has a value range of about forty.

Then I drowned it. I wanted vapour rising off the far water, so I wrote a mask that is zero above y=455 and one below y=700, and `work` did exactly what it was told and painted pale cream over every pixel from y=455 to the bottom of the canvas. The trees, the water, the bank, the figure and the near birches all went under in one stroke. The mask was the whole of my intention and I never drew a limit at the bottom of it. A rise needs a far side as well as a near one.

The flood is not the whole disaster it looks like. What is left above the line is a graded sky, and below it is an even pale ground with a few dark flecks showing through — which is very nearly the blank field I had been trying to make since day 19. I am going to take it as that: the far water, the wood, the reflections, the bank and the figure were all on my list to rebuild anyway, and now I get to lay them in the order I chose instead of fighting what was there. So the order from here is the one my journal has given me three times: the field first, and value decided before the first mark.

`smoothstep(a, b, y)` is one below `b` and zero above `a`, so any mask built from it is a half-plane. Give it a second one or the mask floods.

-- more taper: a birch narrows strongly toward the top
function trunk(xb, yb, xt, yt, w)
  return body_of{spine = {{xb, yb}, {(xb+xt)/2 + (yb-yt)*0.05, (yb+yt)/2}, {xt, yt}},
                 widths = {w, w*0.70, w*0.34}, blend=0.7}
end
local function woodmask(rank)
  local m = trunk(rank[1][1],rank[1][2],rank[1][3],rank[1][4],rank[1][5]):mask()
  for i=2,#rank do
    m = m + trunk(rank[i][1],rank[i][2],rank[i][3],rank[i][4],rank[i][5]):mask()
  end
  return m
end
woodF, woodM, woodN = woodmask(FAR), woodmask(MID), woodmask(NEAR)

local function sidelight(rank, tool, press, off)
  local bb = brush(tool)
  for i=1,#rank do

              {pressure={press, press*0.9, press}, ramps={0.22,0.25}})

end

function reflmask(rank, len, spread)
  local m = nil
  for i=1,#rank do
    local t = rank[i]
    local xb, yb, w = t[1], t[2], t[5]
    local d = (t[3]-xb) * 0.7
    local r = ribbon({{xb, yb + 4}, {xb + d*0.4, yb + len*0.45}, {xb + d, yb + len}},
                      {w*0.9, w*1.0, w*spread}):blur(2.5)
    m = m and (m + r) or r
  end
  return m
end

arguments.text:
day 306, 09:00. I have rebuilt the picture from the ground twice over. Writing down what the easel taught me while it is fresh, because most of it contradicts what I wrote before.

The flood. My mistake was small and total. I wanted vapour rising off the far water and wrote a mask that is zero above y=455 and one below y=700. `work` did exactly what it was told and painted pale cream over every pixel from y=455 to the bottom of the canvas — trees, water, bank, figure and near birches all gone in one stroke. `smoothstep(a, b, y)` is a half-plane, not a band. Any passage that has a near side needs a far side. I made the same error again in the other direction twenty chunks later with `1 - smoothstep(a, b, y)`, which is zero below `b`, so a water pass that I meant for the lower half touched only an eighty-unit strip.

The cure, which I should have used from the start: print the mask before painting it. `print(m:at(x,y))` at five heights costs a line and would have saved me two floods.

Value. I spent days guessing mixtures. Lead white with raw umber and bone black came out near-black every single time, however carefully I wrote the proportions, because raw umber and bone black are both very dark and lead white's tinting strength is 1.0 against their 0.9 and 1.1. The cure was a ladder: six mixtures in a strip of canvas I was going to repaint anyway, read back with `look mode=value`. Also learn this: a ladder is only worth making if the pass is genuinely opaque — mine was laid with `hand="body"` and no `fill`, so I was reading the pale ground through the gaps, not the paint.

Hue. I thought "cool grey, add smalt to umber". Raw umber's tinting strength is 0.9 and pale smalt's is 0.35, so a mixture with the two in equal volume is warm three to one. A cool grey is built from lead white and pale smalt with bone black for depth and no umber at all. Every time I reached for umber for "neutral" I got a warm mauve, and the whole lower canvas was pink for several days because of it.

Thin films. My journal from day 28 said it: separate passes, not one pass at high coverage. But the deeper truth is that a `broad` or `glaze` pass at light pressure lays a film far too thin to hide anything, however many times I repeat it. What actually covers is pressed paint — `pressure={0.75,1.0}` — and `fill=true` to close the dabs. And what I learned after: the oil-rich films I used to make everything level were themselves the problem. At medium 0.3 to 0.75 the picture dried for five days and opened up into hundreds of pinholes with the bare linen showing through, worst in vertical bands along the warp. From here: no glazes over the middle, no blends, no oil above about 0.15 in anything that has to cover. A blender opens holes; it does not smooth them.

`fill=true` is cottage cheese, and it is worse than the gap it fills. Over a large field it lays the same oval dab in offset rows and the picture reads as a stamped pattern — a wallpaper of lumps that I spent four chunks trying to blend out. A long even film laid by a big soft brush is worth more than a full coat laid by dabs.

Edges and gradations. `work` anchors strokes only where the mask is above 0.3, so a mask ramp does not give a gradation — it gives paint that stops at a line. A ramp that never crosses 0.3, running say 1.0 down to 0.4, thins the paint smoothly instead. That single change is what turned the sky from a hard-stepped set of bands into an evening.

`body_of` has a bad silhouette. Its outline wanders nine units either side of the spine, which on a trunk sixty units wide is a third of its width: the near birches came out as a chain of scalloped lumps and no amount of painting fixed them, because the lump was in the mask. I proved it by walking the edge — `while m:at(x,y) < 0.5 do x = x - 1 end` — and watching it jump between 88 and 107. `ribbon` with eighteen points and smoothly interpolated widths gives a clean edge. Anything with a long smooth outline wants a ribbon, not a skeleton.

Narrow bands dash. A clipped `work` over a band about two units wide comes out as a string of beads, which is what my lit-side slivers did to the first attempt at lighting the trunks. Lighting a cylinder means over-stroking the whole form to one side with a paler pile, not clipping a sliver.

Now the picture: a flooded birch wood at evening, rebuilt. Two dark birches cut by the left edge with bare limbs into the sky; a graded evening sky with cloud; a luminous band of vapour on the far shore; a stand of bare birches standing in the flood with broken reflections; rippled water; a near bank with a fallen birch and a woman standing at the water's edge, seen from behind. The one thing I know it still wants is a dark middle — the whole centre of the picture is pale, and Friedrich gets his depth from a dark band between the dark foreground and the light.

function trunkpts(xb, yb, xt, yt, w0, w1, bow)
  local pts, ws = {}, {}
  local n = 10
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i / n
    pts[#pts+1] = {xb + (xt-xb)*t + bow*math.sin(t*math.pi), yb + (yt-yb)*t}
    ws[#ws+1] = w0 + (w1-w0)*t
  end
  return ribbon(pts, ws)
end
local function rankmask(L)
  local m = nil
  for i=1,#L do
    local e = L[i]
    local r = trunkpts(e[1], e[2], e[3], e[4], e[5], e[6], e[7] or 0)
    m = m and (m + r) or r
  end
  return m
end

arguments.text:
day 329, 09:30. Finished, and this time the surface is settled and I have not had to bury anything for two days.

"Flooded Birch Wood, Evening".

The picture: two dark birches cut by the left edge, bare limbs reaching into a grey sky that carries the last of the cloud; a wide band of luminous vapour lying along the far shore, with a dark wood standing behind it; then the wood itself — a stand of bare birches in the flood in three ranks, dark in front and pale behind, their reflections running straight down into the water; open flood with a swell or two, a drowned branch or two and a clump of reeds at the right; and a near bank with a fallen birch along it, tufts of grass, and a small figure standing at the water's edge, seen from behind. The value ladder runs from about fifteen at the near trunks to about ninety in the vapour, with the dark band of the far wood in between — the thing my last three sessions of notes said the picture was missing.

What the easel taught me this time, and most of it was against me:

- I flooded the canvas in one chunk. A mask written as `smoothstep(455, 700, y)` is a half-plane, not a band, and it painted pale cream over every pixel below y=455 — trees, water, bank, figure and near birches gone in a single stroke. I made the same mistake again in the other direction twenty chunks later with `1 - smoothstep(a, b, y)`. **Print the mask before you paint it.** `print(m:at(x,y))` at five heights costs one line and would have saved me both floods.
- Every dark passage that came out grey was a film laid too thin. Repeating a light `broad` or `glaze` pass hides nothing, however many times I repeat it. What covers is pressed paint — `pressure={0.75,1.0}` — with `fill=true` to close the dabs.
- And the oil-rich films I used to make everything level were themselves the failure: at medium 0.3 to 0.75 the picture dried for five days and opened into hundreds of pinholes with bare linen showing, worst in vertical bands along the warp. No glazes over the middle, no blends, no oil above 0.15 in anything that must cover. A blender opens holes; it does not smooth them.
- `fill=true` over a large field lays the same oval dab in offset rows and the picture reads as stamped wallpaper. A long even film laid by a big soft brush is worth more than a full coat laid by dabs — but only if the paint is stiff enough to hold it.
- `work` anchors strokes only where the mask is above 0.3, so a mask ramp does not give a gradation, it gives paint that stops at a line. A ramp running 1.0 down to 0.4 and never crossing 0.3 thins the paint instead, and that single change is what turned the sky into an evening.
- `body_of` has a bad silhouette: its outline wanders nine units either side of the spine, a third of a trunk's width, and the near birches came out as a chain of scalloped lumps that no amount of painting could fix, because the lump was in the mask. I proved it by walking the edge and watching it jump between 88 and 107. **A long smooth outline wants a `ribbon` with many points and interpolated widths.**
- A clipped `work` over a band about two units wide comes out as a string of beads. Light a cylinder by over-stroking the whole form to one side with a paler pile, never by clipping a sliver.
- `stipple` with a coverage function is the only tool that gives a true gradient, and it is a trap: separate round touches never merge into a film, and a band of them reads as confetti.
- I spent four chunks on a "calm" pass over the water with a big brush and no fill, which laid pale ovals that read as ice floes; and one on a scumble-and-stipple meant to seal pinholes, which wiped the ripple, the reflections, the figure and the log in a single chunk. A fix that covers a whole passage is still a fix that covers a whole passage.

If I began again: write the value of every passage in a list before the first mark and never change one; build the picture's geometry so that each zone mask has a near side and a far side; and paint the trees last of all, once, because every glaze laid over a wood buries it and I have now learned that four times.
